posts.text: I bumped into this young bobcat on my local mountain bike trail recently - first time I've seen one of these beautiful creatures out in the wild. The pic is a little fuzzy because it was late in the day and my iphone struggled to focus on its natural camouflage. I gave it some time to run off the trail before I continued, keeping an eye out for a protective parental unit - I had a feeling that mom was nearby. Watching this young one on the trail, learning how to make its way in the world got me thinking about some of the bright young talent that I've hired and coached over the years. These days I see junior engineers becoming demoralized as attention shifts toward AI. People who still have important work to do are starting to feel secondary to the tools and recent computer science grads are struggling to find their first jobs. The shift to AI means, at least in theory, that we can do more with less people, but if we stop hiring junior engineers because AI can do their work, where will our next senior engineers come from? Our senior engineers will eventually move on. Some will retire. Others will take different roles outside your company. Who will be ready to replace them and how do we prevent the loss of their critical domain knowledge? Junior engineers need opportunities to work through problems, learn from experienced colleagues and take on increasing responsibility. Building software is part of that development, but so is learning how to dive deep into requirements, troubleshoot a production issue, handle oncall operations and work with engineers across team/org boundaries to get things done. I’ve spent years building engineering teams, developing leaders and coaching/mentoring junior talent to take on increasingly complex and impactful work. If AI changes the work juniors can contribute, we need to rethink how we develop them. For engineering leaders, this should be part of our AI adoption plan. We still need to hire and develop the people who will lead what comes next. Your thoughts?

posts.text: The median Anthropic employee spends 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Even technical individual contributors spend 16% more time in meetings. Anthropic published a report last week on how work has changed inside the company. They put it together from their own data: hiring, calendars and Slack. It's no secret Anthropic has grown a lot, and that's probably a big part of the spike in meetings. But I think another part is that as you create more and move faster, getting aligned becomes even more important. Many of the other numbers point the same way: ↳ Interactive Claude sessions spend around 80% of their time sitting idle, waiting for a human to respond. One engineer put it as people "bottlenecking the agents." ↳ Meta-work, which is basically setting up and keeping an eye on agents instead of doing the task yourself, went from 10% of the average employee's Claude sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. In an April survey, 20% of employees said their role shifted from doing work to managing Claudes, and one engineer said it feels like facing "an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention." ↳ There are around 17 engineers for every PM now, and that ratio's gone up since 2025. The share of people on technical teams who aren't actively coding fell by almost half, and commits from managers doubled. ↳ On hiring, juniors went from 27% of technical hires to 9%, and junior roles are just 6% of technical openings now. Around a third of ML managers and a fifth of software engineering managers said they're hiring less because of AI. ↳ Agents show up in nearly half of active public Slack channels. The report calls private work in DMs and unlogged meetings "invisible, confusing and discouraged," and one researcher said "leaders have to defend feedback out in the open." One non-technical employee said "that 20% that was strategic becomes 90% of the job." My read is that AI made a lot of the work cheap. What's scarce now is people's attention and judgment, plus the trust you still build face to face in all those extra meetings, which is basically the job leaders already had. Somebody has to decide which agent output gets a human read, because nobody can read all of it. Somebody has to figure out where judgment comes from when way fewer junior employees get hired, and even the authors admit none of their fixes "directly address the slowdown in junior hires." And since agents only know about decisions that get written down, feedback that used to live in a DM needs a more public home, which I'd guess many leaders find uncomfortable. And to be clear, Anthropic is not a normal company. They build frontier models and use them daily; the company tripled in size in the last year, and the authors say many of its employment practices can't be replicated across the economy. Still, it's the clearest look I've seen at what happens when agents do a lot of the work. And most of what got harder is the people stuff.
